blocks.robotComment: Buttons, forms, popups — almost everything that reacts on a webpage is JavaScript at work. Let's meet it. ⚡
blocks.body: JavaScript is a programming language that runs in every major web browser, making web pages interactive instead of just static documents. It's what lets a page respond when you click a button, validate a form before you submit it, update content without reloading, or pop up a menu — all the things that make a website feel alive.

The web is usually described as three layers working together: HTML provides the structure and content of a page, CSS controls how it looks (colors, layout, fonts), and JavaScript controls how it behaves. A page can exist with just HTML and CSS, but it would be completely static — nothing would happen when you interacted with it.

code.caption: This snippet listens for a click and reacts immediately — the kind of behavior JavaScript adds to a page that HTML and CSS alone cannot.

blocks.robotComment: Browser-only was just the beginning — Node.js blew that door wide open. 🚪
blocks.body: JavaScript was originally created to run only inside web browsers. But since 2009, a runtime called Node.js has let JavaScript run outside the browser too — on servers, in command-line tools, and even to build entire applications. That means learning JavaScript opens the door to far more than just web pages.

blocks.sentence: JavaScript was originally designed to run inside a ___, but thanks to Node.js it can now run outside one too.
blocks.explanation: JavaScript started as a browser-only language, but runtimes like Node.js later let it run on servers and elsewhere outside the browser.

blocks.question: Which of these best describes the role of JavaScript on a web page, compared to HTML and CSS?
options: JavaScript adds interactivity and behavior, while HTML provides structure and CSS provides style
JavaScript styles the page, while HTML adds interactivity
JavaScript and HTML do exactly the same job
CSS handles all logic and interactivity
blocks.explanation: HTML = structure, CSS = style, JavaScript = behavior. Together these three layers make up most of what you see and use on the web.

blocks.robotComment: Think about where you just read JavaScript can run before you answer this one. 🤔
blocks.statement: JavaScript can only run inside a web browser.
blocks.explanation: Thanks to runtimes like Node.js, JavaScript can also run on servers, desktops, and command-line tools outside the browser.

blocks.body: Today, JavaScript is one of the most widely used programming languages in the world. If a website does anything beyond just displaying text and images, there's a very good chance JavaScript is running behind the scenes to make it happen.

blocks.robotComment: Every browser has its own engine quietly running your code under the hood. 🔧
blocks.body: Every browser (and Node.js) runs JavaScript using a JavaScript engine — a program built into the browser that reads your code and carries out its instructions. Chrome and Node.js both use an engine called V8; Firefox uses SpiderMonkey, and Safari uses JavaScriptCore. Each engine understands the same JavaScript language, just with its own internal implementation.

Unlike Java, which you compile ahead of time into bytecode before you can run it, JavaScript is interpreted: the engine reads and runs your code directly, without you performing a separate compile step first. Modern engines like V8 actually use a technique called JIT (Just-In-Time) compilation behind the scenes to make this fast — but from where you sit, you simply write code and run it immediately.

code.code: console.log('This runs immediately — no separate compile step needed.');
code.caption: There is no build step you have to trigger yourself here — the engine reads this line and executes it right away.

blocks.sentence: The program that reads and executes your JavaScript code is called a ___.
blocks.explanation: Browsers and Node.js each contain a JavaScript engine (such as V8) that reads your code and carries out its instructions.

blocks.robotComment: One thing at a time, in order — no juggling required. 🎯
blocks.body: JavaScript also runs on a single thread, which means it can only do one thing at a time — executing your code line by line, in order. This is simpler to reason about than juggling many things simultaneously, but it also means one slow piece of code can delay everything else until it finishes running.

blocks.question: Which engine does Google Chrome and Node.js use to run JavaScript?
blocks.explanation: V8 is the JavaScript engine developed by Google, used in both the Chrome browser and Node.js.

blocks.robotComment: Reread how JavaScript actually gets from source code to running code. 🧐
blocks.statement: JavaScript must be compiled ahead of time into a separate file before it can run, just like Java.
blocks.explanation: JavaScript is interpreted, with JIT compilation happening automatically behind the scenes — you don't run a separate compile step yourself before executing it.

blocks.body: JavaScript's single-threaded, line-by-line nature is one reason it later grew features like callbacks and promises for handling slow operations (like fetching data) without freezing the rest of the page — but that's a topic for a later level.

blocks.robotComment: Ten days. That's genuinely wild for a language this influential. ⏱️
blocks.body: JavaScript has one of the most famously rushed origin stories in programming. In 1995, a Netscape engineer named Brendan Eich was asked to design a scripting language for the Netscape Navigator browser — and he built the very first version of it in just 10 days.

blocks.question: Roughly how long did it take Brendan Eich to create the first version of JavaScript?
blocks.explanation: Brendan Eich built the first version of JavaScript at Netscape in just 10 days in 1995.

blocks.body: The name "JavaScript" is actually a bit of a marketing move — the language has almost nothing to do with Java. Java was extremely popular at the time, so Netscape chose a similar-sounding name to ride that popularity, even though the two languages have very different designs.

blocks.sentence: JavaScript was named partly to ride the popularity of the ___ programming language, despite the two being very different under the hood.
blocks.explanation: Netscape chose the name "JavaScript" as a marketing move to associate it with the already-popular Java, despite the languages being unrelated in design.

blocks.body: For years, every browser maker implemented JavaScript slightly differently, which was a nightmare for developers. That changed once the language was standardized under the name ECMAScript, with browser vendors gradually converging on the same rules. Since 2015, a new ECMAScript version has been released every year, each adding features to the language.

blocks.robotComment: One project, one huge shift in what JavaScript could be used for. 🌍
blocks.body: In 2009, Node.js changed everything again: it let JavaScript run outside the browser for the first time, on servers and in command-line tools, using the same V8 engine that powers Chrome. That single project is a big part of why JavaScript is now used for so much more than just websites.

blocks.robotComment: This mix-up trips a lot of people up — think back to what you just read before you answer. 🤔
blocks.statement: JavaScript and Java are essentially the same language under different names.
blocks.explanation: Despite the similar name — chosen largely for marketing reasons in 1995 — JavaScript and Java are unrelated languages with very different designs.

blocks.robotComment: Time to put your very first line of JavaScript onto an actual webpage. 🚀
blocks.body: Every browser ships with a built-in JavaScript engine, so there's nothing to install to start running JavaScript — you just need a way to get your code onto a page. The most common way is the <script> tag, placed inside an HTML file.

code.caption: Code written directly between opening and closing <script> tags runs as soon as the browser reaches this point in the page.

blocks.robotComment: Splitting your JavaScript into its own file keeps things tidy as a project grows. 🗃️
blocks.body: Writing JavaScript directly inside a <script> tag works fine for tiny experiments, but most real projects keep their JavaScript in a separate file (often named something like script.js) and link it into the HTML instead. This keeps HTML and JavaScript organized and lets the same script be reused across multiple pages.

code.caption: The src attribute points to an external file containing your JavaScript — the browser downloads and runs it in place of this tag.

blocks.sentence: To link an external JavaScript file to an HTML page, you use a <script> tag with a ___ attribute pointing to the file.
blocks.explanation: The src ("source") attribute tells the browser which file to download and run as JavaScript.

blocks.question: Why do many developers prefer linking an external .js file instead of writing JavaScript directly inside a <script> tag?
options: It keeps HTML and JavaScript organized and reusable across multiple pages
It is the only way browsers are able to execute JavaScript
It runs the code twice as fast in every case
blocks.explanation: Separating JavaScript into its own file keeps a project organized and lets the same script be shared across several HTML pages.

blocks.robotComment: Think back to what you needed to install to get any of this working. 🤔
blocks.statement: Every modern web browser has a built-in JavaScript engine, so users don't need to install anything extra to run JavaScript on a webpage.
blocks.explanation: Browsers ship with their own JavaScript engine (like V8 in Chrome), so JavaScript just works out of the box for anyone visiting a page.

blocks.body: You'll often see <script> tags placed near the end of the <body>, right before it closes. That way the browser finishes loading the page's visible content first, before it starts downloading and running the JavaScript.

blocks.robotComment: Every browser hides a debugging toolkit behind one keypress. Let's go find it. 🔍
blocks.body: Every browser includes a set of built-in Developer Tools for inspecting, testing, and debugging what's happening on a web page. You can open them by pressing F12, or by right-clicking anywhere on a page and choosing "Inspect."

One of the most useful panels inside Developer Tools is the Console tab. It shows messages that JavaScript running on the page has logged, along with any errors or warnings — and it also works as a live JavaScript prompt where you can type code and run it immediately.

code.caption: console.log() prints a message to the Console tab — the most common way developers check what their code is doing.

blocks.robotComment: You'll type console.log() more than almost any other line of code. Get comfortable with it. 📝
blocks.body: console.log() can print numbers, text, variables, or several values at once separated by commas. Sprinkling console.log() calls through your code is one of the simplest and most common ways to 'peek inside' a program while it runs and see exactly what's happening.

code.caption: Passing multiple values to console.log() prints them together, separated by a space, which is handy for labeling what a number means.

blocks.sentence: The browser panel used to inspect, test, and debug code on a web page is called ___.
blocks.explanation: Developer Tools (often opened with F12) is the built-in browser panel that includes the Console and other debugging features.

blocks.question: Which function is most commonly used to print messages to the browser console for debugging?
blocks.explanation: console.log() is the standard way to print values to the Console tab so you can see what your code is doing.

blocks.robotComment: Think back to everything the Console tab does, not just what it shows you. 💡
blocks.statement: You can type and run JavaScript directly inside the Console tab of Developer Tools.
blocks.explanation: The Console isn't just for output — it's also a live JavaScript prompt where you can type and immediately run code.

blocks.robotComment: Every programmer's journey starts here — even mine, technically. 🤖
blocks.body: By tradition, the very first program you write in a new language simply prints "Hello, World!" — a small way to confirm everything is set up and working before you move on to anything more complicated. In JavaScript, that program is a single line.

code.caption: This one line prints Hello, World! to the console — traditionally the first program written in any language.

blocks.body: You can run this two different ways. Open a browser's Developer Tools, click the Console tab, type the line in, and press Enter to see it run instantly. Or, save it inside a .js file and link it into an HTML page with a <script> tag (or run it with Node.js) so it executes automatically when the page loads.

blocks.robotComment: Quotes aren't decoration here — they're what makes text text. 📖
blocks.body: Notice that "Hello, World!" is wrapped in quotation marks. In JavaScript, text like this is called a string, and it must be wrapped in matching quotes — either single (') or double (") — so the engine knows where the text begins and ends.

blocks.sentence: In JavaScript, text values like "Hello, World!" must be wrapped in matching ___ marks.
blocks.explanation: Text values (strings) in JavaScript must be wrapped in matching quotation marks — either single or double — so the engine knows where the text starts and ends.

blocks.question: What will console.log("Hello, World!") print?
blocks.explanation: console.log() prints the text content of the string exactly as written, without the surrounding quotation marks.

blocks.robotComment: Remember what the Console tab can actually do before answering this one. 🖥️
blocks.statement: You can only run a Hello World program by saving it in a file — typing it directly into the browser console doesn't work.
blocks.explanation: The Console tab runs JavaScript immediately as you type it, so you can run console.log("Hello, World!") there without any file at all.

blocks.body: Try changing the message inside the quotes and running it again — Hello World is meant to be experimented with, not just typed once and forgotten.

blocks.robotComment: Notes to your future self are one of the most underrated tools in coding. 📝
blocks.body: A comment is a note written directly in your code that the JavaScript engine completely ignores when it runs. Comments exist purely for people — to explain what a piece of code does, why it's written a certain way, or to leave yourself a reminder.

code.code:
// This line calculates the total price
let total = price * quantity;
code.caption: Everything after // on a line is a single-line comment — the engine skips right over it.

blocks.body: That's a single-line comment, made with two forward slashes (//). Everything from // to the end of that line is ignored. For longer notes, or for text that spans several lines, JavaScript also has multi-line comments, which start with /* and end with */.

code.code:
/*
  This function calculates a discount.
  It takes the original price and a percentage off.
*/
code.caption: Multi-line comments start with /* and end with */ — everything between them is ignored, no matter how many lines it spans.

blocks.robotComment: Commenting out code is basically a pause button, not a delete button. ⏸️
blocks.body: Multi-line comments are also handy for temporarily disabling a block of code without deleting it — a trick often called "commenting out" code — which is useful while you're testing or debugging.

blocks.sentence: A single-line comment in JavaScript starts with ___.
blocks.explanation: Two forward slashes (//) start a single-line comment — everything after them on that line is ignored by the engine.

blocks.question: Which symbols mark the start and end of a multi-line comment in JavaScript?
blocks.explanation: Multi-line comments begin with /* and end with */, and can span as many lines as needed in between.

blocks.robotComment: Think about who comments are actually written for. 🤔
blocks.statement: The JavaScript engine executes the text inside comments as part of the program.
blocks.explanation: Comments are ignored entirely by the engine — they exist only to help people reading the code.

blocks.body: Good comments explain why code exists or why a choice was made, not just what it does — code that simply restates the obvious ("// add one to x") tends to clutter a file rather than help anyone reading it.

blocks.robotComment: Variables are where your code starts remembering things. Let's give it something to hold onto. 📦
blocks.body: A variable is a named container that stores a piece of data your program can work with and change while it runs. In JavaScript, you declare a reassignable variable with the let keyword — and unlike Java, you never declare a type. JavaScript is dynamically typed, so the same variable can hold a number today and something else entirely later.

blocks.robotComment: Forget to assign a value and JavaScript won't error — it just hands you undefined. 🤷
blocks.body: The general pattern is: let name = value;. You can also declare a variable without giving it a value right away, and assign one later — but if you log it before assigning anything, you'll see the special value undefined rather than an error.

code.caption: Declaring age with let, then reassigning it to a new value — no need to write let again.

blocks.body: Variable names must start with a letter, an underscore (_), or a dollar sign ($) — never a digit — and cannot be one of JavaScript's reserved keywords (like let or const itself). Names are case-sensitive, so score and Score are two different variables. By convention, JavaScript developers write variable names in camelCase: the first word lowercase, each following word capitalized, e.g. totalScore or firstName.

blocks.sentence: In JavaScript, variable names conventionally use ___, where the first word is lowercase and every following word starts with a capital letter, such as totalScore.
blocks.explanation: JavaScript's naming convention for variables (and functions) is camelCase — lowercase first word, capitalized following words, no underscores.

blocks.body: Curly braces {} mark out a block — the body of an if statement, a for loop, a while loop, or a function. A variable declared with let is block-scoped, meaning it only exists inside the nearest enclosing pair of {} where it was declared. Once that block ends, the variable is gone.

code.caption: message only exists inside the if block — trying to use it afterward throws an error.

blocks.question: What happens if you try to use a variable declared with let outside the block {} where it was declared?
options: The variable is still accessible with its last value
JavaScript automatically makes it a global variable
blocks.explanation: let is block-scoped — once the enclosing {} ends, the variable no longer exists, and referencing it throws a ReferenceError.

blocks.robotComment: Reread the reassignment example above before you answer this one. 🔍
blocks.statement: Once you declare a variable with let, you must write the word let again every time you give it a new value.
blocks.explanation: You only write let once, at declaration. After that, you simply write variableName = newValue; without repeating let.

blocks.body: Sometimes a value should never change once it's set — think of the number of days in a week, or a configuration value your program relies on. JavaScript lets you declare this kind of variable with const. A const variable cannot be reassigned after its initial value is set, and — unlike let — it must be given a value at the very moment it's declared.

code.caption: daysInWeek is initialized immediately, since const requires a value right at declaration.

blocks.robotComment: Try to reassign a const and JavaScript won't let you forget it. 🚫
blocks.code:
const daysInWeek = 7;
daysInWeek = 8; // TypeError: Assignment to constant variable.
blocks.caption: Reassigning a const throws an error as soon as this line runs.

blocks.robotComment: const-by-default is one of those habits that quietly prevents whole categories of bugs. 🛡️
blocks.body: Many JavaScript developers reach for const by default, and only switch to let when they know a variable truly needs to be reassigned later. This makes code easier to read: seeing const tells anyone reading it that the value is locked in for good, which helps prevent accidental reassignment bugs.

blocks.sentence: By default, many JavaScript developers prefer ___ over let, and only switch when a variable needs to be reassigned.
blocks.explanation: const communicates that a value is not meant to change, so it is the safer default choice unless reassignment is actually needed.

blocks.body: Here's the critical catch: const only protects the variable binding itself — it does not freeze the value's contents. If a const variable holds an object or array, you cannot reassign the variable to a different object or array, but you can still change what's inside it.

code.caption: push() mutates the array in place — this is allowed because the array itself isn't being reassigned, only its contents change.

blocks.question: Which of these is allowed for an array assigned to a const variable?
options: Changing the contents of the array, like pushing a new item
Reassigning the const variable to point to a brand-new array
Declaring it without giving it an initial value
Redeclaring it with let in the same scope
blocks.explanation: const blocks reassigning the variable itself, but the array's contents are still fully mutable.

blocks.robotComment: Remember what const actually locks — the variable, or the value inside it? 🔐
blocks.statement: Because scores is declared with const, calling scores.push(30) will throw an error.
blocks.explanation: const prevents reassigning the scores variable to a new value — it does not prevent mutating the array's contents, so push() works fine.

blocks.robotComment: Almost every program you'll ever write needs to work with text somewhere. This is where that starts. 📝
blocks.body: Strings hold text. JavaScript gives you three ways to write a string literal: single quotes 'Hi', double quotes "Hi", and backticks `Hi` — all three produce a string. Unlike Java, JavaScript has no separate character type: a single letter like 'A' is simply a string with a length of 1.

code.caption: Three equivalent ways to write a string literal — pick one style and stay consistent.

blocks.robotComment: Interpolation is one of those features that makes you never want to go back. ✨
blocks.body: Backtick strings are called template literals, and they have a superpower: you can embed expressions directly inside them using ${ } — called interpolation — without gluing pieces together with +.

code.caption: The value of name is inserted directly into the template literal.

blocks.body: The + operator concatenates (joins) strings together. Whenever at least one side of + is a string, JavaScript converts the other side to text and joins them, rather than performing addition.

code.caption: + joins strings end to end, and automatically converts a number to text when one side is already a string.

blocks.sentence: Backtick strings, called ___ literals, let you embed expressions directly inside ${ }.
blocks.explanation: Template literals (written with backticks) support ${ } interpolation, unlike single- or double-quoted strings.

blocks.question: What does 'Hello, ' + 'World' produce?
blocks.explanation: + joins the two strings exactly as written, including the space already inside the first string.

blocks.robotComment: Think back to what a single letter like 'A' actually is in JavaScript. 🔤
blocks.statement: JavaScript has a separate type for a single character, just like Java's char.
blocks.explanation: JavaScript has no char type — a single character is just a string of length 1.

blocks.robotComment: One number type to rule them all — no int vs double juggling here. 🔢
blocks.body: JavaScript has just one numeric type, called number, covering both whole numbers and decimals. Unlike Java, there's no separate int vs double — 5, 5.0, and 5.5 are all simply a number.

code.caption: typeof reports the same type, "number", for both the whole number and the decimal.

blocks.body: The basic arithmetic operators are + (add), - (subtract), * (multiply), / (divide), % (remainder, also called modulo), and ** (exponent).

code.caption: Division always keeps decimals, since JavaScript has no separate whole-number division like Java's int / int.

blocks.robotComment: NaN might be the most confusingly-named value in JavaScript. Buckle up. 😵
blocks.body: NaN stands for "Not a Number" — a special number value produced by an invalid math operation, such as dividing zero by zero or trying to do arithmetic with something that has no meaningful numeric value. Confusingly, typeof NaN is itself "number".

code.caption: Both operations fail to produce a meaningful number, so JavaScript returns NaN.

blocks.sentence: Dividing zero by zero, or performing math on non-numeric data, produces the special value ___.
blocks.explanation: NaN ("Not a Number") is the result JavaScript gives for a numeric operation that fails to produce a real number.

blocks.question: Which statement about JavaScript's number type is true?
options: JavaScript has a single number type for both whole and decimal numbers
JavaScript has separate int and double types like Java
Numbers must be declared with a type keyword
Dividing two whole numbers always produces another whole number
blocks.explanation: JavaScript uses one number type for all numeric values — there's no int/double distinction to manage.

blocks.robotComment: Think back to how many numeric types JavaScript actually has. 🧮
blocks.statement: In JavaScript, 5 and 5.0 are stored using the exact same number type.
blocks.explanation: JavaScript has only one numeric type, so there is no difference in type between a whole number and its decimal-looking equivalent.

blocks.robotComment: Just two values, endless uses — booleans are deceptively powerful. ✅
blocks.body: A boolean has only two possible values: true and false. Booleans are perfect for representing yes/no or on/off states, and they are commonly the result of a comparison.

code.caption: Two boolean variables, one true and one false.

blocks.body: Comparison operators like ===, !==, >, <, >=, and <= evaluate to a boolean, making them the most common way booleans show up in real code.

code.caption: Each comparison produces a boolean result.

blocks.robotComment: Only six falsy values exist in all of JavaScript — worth memorizing them. 📋
blocks.body: JavaScript also treats every value as either "truthy" or "falsy" whenever a boolean is expected, such as inside an if condition. There are exactly six falsy values: false, 0, "" (empty string), null, undefined, and NaN. Every other value — including "0" as a string, or an empty array [] — is truthy.

code.caption: The empty string is falsy, so the first block is skipped; the non-empty string is truthy, so the second runs.

blocks.sentence: A value that behaves like false in a boolean context, such as 0 or an empty string, is called ___.
blocks.explanation: Falsy values (false, 0, "", null, undefined, NaN) act like false whenever JavaScript expects a boolean.

blocks.question: Which of these values is falsy in JavaScript?
blocks.explanation: The number 0 is one of the six falsy values. A non-empty string like "0" or "false", and even an empty array [], are all truthy.

blocks.robotComment: Only one of the six falsy values is a string — which one was it? 🔍
blocks.statement: An empty string '' is falsy, but a string containing any character, like 'no', is truthy.
blocks.explanation: Only the empty string is falsy — any string with at least one character, even "no" or "false", is truthy.

blocks.robotComment: null looks like nothing, but it's a value you choose on purpose — that's the whole trick to it. 🕳️
blocks.body: null is a special value that represents the intentional absence of any value. You assign it yourself to explicitly say "this variable has no value on purpose."

highlights.text: this variable has no value on purpose

code.caption: null explicitly marks "no value" rather than leaving the variable unset.

blocks.robotComment: This one's a genuine bug that's been frozen in place since the 90s. 🐛
blocks.body: null is one of JavaScript's primitive values, but oddly, typeof null returns "object" — a long-standing bug baked into the language from its earliest days. It can never be fixed without breaking huge amounts of existing code, so it's best to just memorize it as a quirk.

code.caption: A famous historical JavaScript quirk — null itself is not actually an object.

blocks.body: Use null when you want to clearly signal that a value is absent by design — for example, resetting a variable, or representing "no selection yet." This makes your intent much clearer to future readers than simply leaving something unassigned.

blocks.sentence: typeof null returns the string ___, which is a well-known quirk since null is not actually an object.
blocks.explanation: This has been true since the earliest versions of JavaScript and remains unfixed to preserve backward compatibility.

blocks.question: What does null represent?
options: A variable that was never assigned
blocks.explanation: null is explicitly assigned by a developer to mean "no value here, on purpose."

blocks.robotComment: You literally just read what typeof null returns — trust that. 😉
blocks.statement: typeof null correctly returns the string 'null'.
blocks.explanation: typeof null actually returns "object" — a famous, long-standing bug in JavaScript.

blocks.robotComment: undefined is JavaScript's default answer for 'nothing here yet.' 📭
blocks.body: undefined is the value JavaScript automatically gives to a variable that has been declared but not yet assigned a value. It means "nothing has been put here yet" — and unlike null, you rarely assign it yourself.

highlights.text: nothing has been put here yet

code.caption: score was declared with let but never given a value, so JavaScript reports it as undefined.

blocks.body: undefined also shows up automatically in other places — for example, when you access an object property that doesn't exist, or call a function that doesn't explicitly return anything.

code.caption: Accessing a missing property returns undefined instead of causing an error.

blocks.robotComment: undefined vs null is one of the most-asked questions about JavaScript. Now you know. 🎓
blocks.body: The key difference: undefined means a value was never assigned — it's JavaScript's own default for "empty." null means a developer deliberately set "no value" on purpose. Think of undefined as "empty by default" and null as "emptied intentionally."

code.caption: a was simply never given a value; b was explicitly set to null.

blocks.sentence: A variable that has been declared but never given a value automatically holds ___.
blocks.explanation: JavaScript automatically assigns undefined to any declared variable that has not yet been given a value.

blocks.question: What is the key difference between null and undefined?

They are exactly the same in every way

blocks.explanation: undefined is JavaScript's automatic "not yet assigned" state, while null is an intentional, developer-assigned "no value."

blocks.robotComment: Think about what a missing property actually looks like when you log it. 🔎
blocks.statement: Accessing a property that doesn't exist on an object returns undefined rather than causing an error.
blocks.explanation: JavaScript returns undefined for missing properties instead of throwing an error, which is different from many other languages.

blocks.robotComment: Values change type more often than you'd think — sometimes on purpose, sometimes not. 🔄
blocks.body: Type conversion means changing a value from one type to another. JavaScript lets you do this explicitly using built-in functions, or it can happen implicitly (automatically) behind the scenes — sometimes with surprising results.

code.caption: String(), Number(), and Boolean() explicitly convert a value to the given type.

blocks.body: A few Number() conversion rules worth knowing: converting an empty string gives 0, converting a non-numeric string like "hello" gives NaN, and converting true or false gives 1 or 0.

code.caption: Number() follows consistent, if occasionally surprising, rules for each type.

blocks.robotComment: Implicit coercion is where a lot of 'weird JavaScript' jokes come from — but the rules are actually consistent. 😅
blocks.body: Implicit coercion is a common source of confusion. The + operator concatenates as text whenever either side is a string — but other math operators, like -, always try to convert both sides to numbers first.

code.caption: + prefers concatenation when a string is involved, but - always coerces both sides to numbers.

blocks.sentence: Because - always converts both sides to numbers, the expression "5" - 1 evaluates to ___.
blocks.explanation: - coerces both operands to numbers first: the string "5" becomes 5, then 5 - 1 is 4.

blocks.question: What does "5" + 1 evaluate to?
blocks.explanation: + concatenates whenever one side is already a string, turning the number 1 into text and joining it.

blocks.robotComment: You just saw Number() handle a non-numeric string a few blocks back. 🔙
blocks.statement: Number('hello') evaluates to NaN because 'hello' cannot be converted into a meaningful number.
blocks.explanation: Any non-numeric string that Number() cannot parse into a valid number becomes NaN.
